title: At the supermarket
goal: Shop for groceries, give amounts and measures, and use *nogle*, *noget* and *nogen*.
bekal: name measures: *et kilo*, *en liter*, *et par*, *en pakke*
shop in a store and ask where things are
wave: Review **unit 12** first: describe today's weather, yesterday's weather and winter weather in your country — six sentences, out loud.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Indkøb til aftensmad
dialogs.intro: Budi is shopping at Netto. He's looking for a few things and asks a staff member.

lines.speaker: Ansat:
lines.text: Ris? Reol fire, sammen med pasta og mel.
lines.id: Rice? Aisle four, with the pasta and flour.
lines.literal: rice? shelf four, together with pasta and flour.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thanks. Do you have coconut milk too?

lines.speaker: Ansat:
lines.text: Ja, i den asiatiske afdeling. Nederste hylde.
lines.id: Yes, in the Asian section. Bottom shelf.
lines.literal: yes, in the Asian section. lowest shelf.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Perfect. And how much is the chicken?

lines.speaker: Ansat:
lines.text: Niogfyrre kroner per kilo. Den er på tilbud i dag.
lines.id: Forty-nine kroner a kilo. It's on sale today.
lines.literal: nine-and-forty kroner per kilo. it is on offer today.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Så tager jeg to. Har I nogle friske grøntsager?
lines.id: Then I'll take two. Do you have any fresh vegetables?
lines.literal: then take I two. have you(pl.) some fresh vegetables?

lines.speaker: Ansat:
lines.text: Ja, lige derovre. Men vi har ingen mango i dag.
lines.id: Yes, right over there. But we have no mangoes today.
lines.literal: yes, just there-over. but we have no mango today.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det gør ikke noget. Jeg tager nogle løg i stedet.
lines.id: That's okay. I'll take some onions instead.
lines.literal: it does not anything. I take some onions in place.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nej tak, jeg har min egen med.
lines.id: No thanks, I brought my own.
lines.literal: no thanks, I have my own with.

notes: **Hvor står risen?** — remember from unit 11: *at stå* for things standing upright on a shelf. For things lying flat, *at ligge*: *Hvor ligger brødet?*
**Det gør ikke noget** = "that's okay, no problem", literally "it doesn't do anything". A fixed phrase used all the time; don't take it apart.
**Vi har ingen mango** — *ingen* means "no, none" and already contains the negative, so no *ikke* is needed. You can also say *vi har ikke nogen mango*; both are correct, the first is shorter.
**Per kilo.** Everything in Denmark is sold by the kilogram or by the piece, and the price per kilo must be shown on the shelf — very handy for comparing.
**En pose** = plastic bag. In Denmark shopping bags **cost money** and aren't cheap (2-5 kroner), and almost everyone brings their own. *Jeg har min egen med* is a sentence you'll use a lot.
**Egen** = own. It changes like an adjective: *min egen bil*, *mit eget hus*, *mine egne bøger*. One of the few adjectives whose et-form doubles a letter.
**Nederste hylde** — *nederst* (bottom) and *øverst* (top) are very useful in supermarkets and elevators.
**Asiatiske** — notice the *-e* ending because it comes after *den*. Double definiteness again; unit 15 explains it fully.

grammars.title: Nogle, noget, nogen, ingen
body: Four words that sound alike and are often mixed up. The system is actually tidy: what matters is **countable or not**, and **positive sentence or not** — much like English *some* vs *any*.

head: Word
Used for
Example
rows: Har du **nogen** penge? / Jeg har ikke **nogen** penge.

after: A shortcut that works in almost every everyday situation: **nogle** if it's countable and the sentence is positive, **noget** if it's uncountable, **nogen** if the sentence is a question or negative.
*Nogle* and *nogen* sound **almost the same** in speech — both come out as "NOH-uhn". The difference is only in writing, and even Danes often spell them wrong.
*Noget* also means "something" on its own: *Vil du have noget?* (do you want something?), and *ingenting* means "nothing": *Jeg har ingenting.*

grammars.title: Measures and amounts
body: After a measure word, the noun stands **bare** — no article, and usually no plural ending.
after: *Et par* literally means "a pair", but in everyday use it means "two or three" — just like "a couple of". *Et par dage* = a couple of days.

⚠️ Denmark is fully metric. The only non-metric measures, like *en pægl*, disappeared long ago. But watch the commas and periods — Danes write *1.000* for a thousand and *1,5* for one and a half, the opposite of English.

blocks.text: *Æg* doesn't change in the plural: *et æg, to æg*. Likewise *en fisk, to fisk* — though *fisker* is also used when you mean several different kinds of fish.

blocks.text: *Det var det* literally means "that was that" — the standard way to finish an order, in shops and cafés alike. You'll hear it at the checkout all the time.

blocks.title: Shopping in Denmark: what the phrasebook doesn't tell you
items: **Pant.** Drink bottles and cans carry a deposit (1-3 kroner) that you get back by feeding them into the *pantautomat* machine at the supermarket. Don't throw empty bottles away.
**Bags cost money.** Bring your own. The line: *Nej tak, jeg har min egen med.*
**Fast cashiers.** Danish cashiers work very fast and expect you to pack while they scan. Standing still and waiting will make the line pile up.
